item.passage:
Transcript: Suppose you want to know when the last large earthquake struck a fault that no instrument was watching. Written records won't help if the region was thinly settled, and a radiocarbon date on buried soil gives you a window of a century or more. Trees, it turns out, can do much better.

A tree growing beside a fault keeps an annual record in its rings. When a major quake shakes the ground, roots tear, the trunk may tilt, and the tree spends the next few years growing slowly while it repairs itself. Those years show up as a run of narrow rings. Count back from the bark, and you have a calendar year for the damage.

Here is the catch, and it's a serious one. A run of narrow rings is not a signature of earthquakes. Droughts produce them. So do insect outbreaks, and a severe winter can stunt a whole stand for a season. A single tree with a thin patch tells you that something went wrong for that tree, nothing more.

So the method depends on comparison, in two directions. First, across distance: trees growing right on the fault trace should show the damage, and trees of the same species a kilometer away, on the same soil, should not. A drought hits both groups; an earthquake hits only one. Second, across kinds of damage: a tilted trunk that starts laying down lopsided rings, as the tree works to straighten itself, is much harder to blame on the weather than a merely thin ring.

When both comparisons agree, the date can be startlingly precise, sometimes down to the season, because the damage may begin partway through a growing year. When they disagree, the honest report is that the trees are silent, and silence is not the same thing as a quiet fault.
item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Geology] Why does the lecturer mention droughts, insect outbreaks, and severe winters?
choices: To show that thin rings alone cannot identify an earthquake
To explain why trees near faults grow more slowly than others
To argue that radiocarbon dates are more reliable than rings
To describe the kinds of damage earthquakes do to tree roots
item.correct_answer: To show that thin rings alone cannot identify an earthquake
item.explanation: Right after them: 'A single tree with a thin patch tells you that something went wrong for that tree, nothing more.'

distractor_rationales.choice: To explain why trees near faults grow more slowly than others
distractor_rationales.reason: Trees near faults are not said to grow slowly in general; damaged ones do for a few years.

distractor_rationales.choice: To argue that radiocarbon dates are more reliable than rings
distractor_rationales.reason: Radiocarbon is described as much less precise.

distractor_rationales.choice: To describe the kinds of damage earthquakes do to tree roots
distractor_rationales.reason: Root damage comes from earthquakes; these are the other causes of thin rings.

item.passage:
Transcript: Auctions look like the purest kind of market. Many buyers, one object, and the price rises until only one bidder is left. Economists used to treat the final price as a clean measure of what the object was worth to the people in the room. Laboratory studies have made that view harder to hold.

Consider the opening bid. In theory it shouldn't matter much; it's just where the climbing starts. But when researchers ran identical auctions with different starting prices, the final prices moved with the start. A high opening figure seemed to tell bidders what the object was worth before any of them had decided for themselves. Psychologists call this anchoring, and auction houses had used it long before anyone named it.

Now, anchoring cuts both ways, and this is the part people forget. Some auction sites deliberately start bidding very low, a dollar for an expensive watch. You'd expect a low anchor to drag the price down. Often it doesn't. A low start attracts more bidders, and once someone has placed a bid, they begin to feel the object is partly theirs. They bid higher to avoid losing it. The low anchor and the feeling of ownership pull in opposite directions, and on busy sites the second one frequently wins.

So what does a final auction price measure? Not nothing. It still reflects what people were willing to pay in that room on that day. But it measures willingness under particular conditions: who opened the bidding, how many rivals joined, how long they had been competing. Change those conditions, and the same object fetches a different price from the same people.

That doesn't make auctions irrational. It makes their prices local, and a careful analyst reports the conditions along with the number.
item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Economics] What is the main point of the lecture?
choices: An auction price depends on how the auction was run, not only on value
Auctions with low opening bids always produce the highest prices
Economists have stopped using auctions to study markets
Auction houses invented anchoring long before psychologists studied it
item.correct_answer: An auction price depends on how the auction was run, not only on value
item.explanation: The price 'measures willingness under particular conditions', so 'a careful analyst reports the conditions along with the number.'

distractor_rationales.choice: Auctions with low opening bids always produce the highest prices
distractor_rationales.reason: Low starts 'frequently' win on busy sites, not always.

distractor_rationales.choice: Economists have stopped using auctions to study markets
distractor_rationales.reason: The lecture refines how auction prices are read, not abandons them.

distractor_rationales.choice: Auction houses invented anchoring long before psychologists studied it
distractor_rationales.reason: This is a side remark, not the point.

item.passage:
Transcript: When a painting turns up without a signature or a reliable history, curators reach for every kind of evidence. Style is the oldest tool and the least trusted, because a skilled follower can imitate a master's brushwork closely enough to fool experts for decades. So in the last thirty years, attention has turned to something no forger thought to fake: the canvas itself.

Linen canvas was woven on hand looms, and every bolt has its own irregular pattern of thread density, slightly more threads per centimeter here, slightly fewer there. Using X-rays, researchers can count those threads across a whole painting and draw a map of the irregularities. Two paintings cut from the same bolt will have maps that line up like the two halves of a torn ticket.

That makes the method very strong in one direction and weak in the other. If an unattributed picture matches a bolt used for three securely documented works by the same artist, that's powerful evidence that it came from the same studio at about the same time. A workshop bought cloth by the bolt and used it up.

But a mismatch proves very little. Artists bought from different suppliers, reused old canvases, and sometimes painted on cloth bought years earlier. Absence of a match is the normal condition, not a warning sign.

Notice, too, what even a match does not settle. It places the painting in a studio. It does not tell us whose hand held the brush, and large studios employed assistants who worked on the same cloth as the master. The canvas can move a painting into a room. It cannot, by itself, tell us who was standing at the easel.
item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Art History] Why have researchers turned to the canvas itself?
choices: Forgers and followers did not think to imitate canvas patterns
Canvas is far easier to examine than the paint on the surface
Style can no longer be studied with X-ray equipment
Signatures are usually hidden beneath the canvas weave
item.correct_answer: Forgers and followers did not think to imitate canvas patterns
item.explanation: Style can be imitated, so attention turned to 'something no forger thought to fake: the canvas itself.'

distractor_rationales.choice: Canvas is far easier to examine than the paint on the surface
distractor_rationales.reason: Ease of examination is never given as the reason.

distractor_rationales.choice: Style can no longer be studied with X-ray equipment
distractor_rationales.reason: X-rays are used on the canvas; style is judged by eye.

distractor_rationales.choice: Signatures are usually hidden beneath the canvas weave
distractor_rationales.reason: The paintings in question lack signatures.

item.passage:
Transcript: A few years ago, a team tried to repeat a hundred published psychology experiments, carefully, with larger samples. Fewer than half produced the original result. The headlines called it a crisis, and in some ways it was. But the lesson most people took from it, that the original researchers were careless or dishonest, is mostly the wrong one.

Start with what journals publish. A study that finds a striking effect is far more likely to be accepted than one that finds nothing. Researchers know this, so studies with null results tend to stay in a drawer. Now imagine twenty labs testing the same weak idea. By chance alone, one of them will probably get a result that looks impressive. That one gets published. The nineteen others don't. Nobody has lied, and yet the published record says the idea works.

There's a second, quieter problem. Small studies produce noisy estimates. When a small study happens to find an effect, the effect it reports is likely to be inflated, because only the lucky overestimates clear the bar for statistical significance. So even when an effect is real, the first published version of it tends to be too large, and a careful repetition will find something smaller, which can look like a failure.

None of this means the field is worthless. It means a single study, especially a small, surprising one, should be treated as a lead rather than a finding. The reforms now spreading, such as registering a study's plan before collecting data and publishing null results, are aimed at the system, not at individual villains. That's the right target, because the system produced the problem without anyone intending it.

choices: That the original researchers were careless or dishonest
That small studies tend to report effects that are too large
That journals favor studies with striking results
That a single study should be treated as a lead
item.correct_answer: That the original researchers were careless or dishonest
item.explanation: 'The lesson most people took from it, that the original researchers were careless or dishonest, is mostly the wrong one.'

distractor_rationales.choice: That small studies tend to report effects that are too large
distractor_rationales.reason: This is one of the lecturer's own explanations.

distractor_rationales.choice: That journals favor studies with striking results
distractor_rationales.reason: This is part of the lecturer's account of the problem.

distractor_rationales.choice: That a single study should be treated as a lead
distractor_rationales.reason: This is the lecturer's recommendation.

item.passage:
Transcript: When wolves were returned to a large national park in the 1990s, the story that followed became famous. With wolves hunting them, elk stopped lingering along rivers. Willows and aspens along the banks grew back, beavers returned to use them, and the rivers themselves were said to change course. It's a beautiful example of what ecologists call a trophic cascade: an effect at the top of a food chain rippling all the way down.

I want to complicate that story, not to debunk it.

First, wolves were not the only thing that changed. Over the same decades, bears and cougars increased, human hunting of elk outside the park continued, and several dry years reduced the forage available. Elk numbers would probably have fallen somewhat even without wolves. Separating the wolves' share of the change from everything else is genuinely hard.

Second, the recovery of the willows has been patchy. In some valleys they came back strongly. In others they're still struggling, even where elk are now scarce. One explanation is that decades of heavy grazing lowered the water table, because there were no beaver dams holding water in the soil. Willows need that water. So removing the elk may not be enough; the ground itself may have to recover first, and that can take a long time.

None of this means the cascade isn't real. There's good evidence that wolves matter. But the tidy version, wolves in, landscape restored, suggests that you can repair a damaged ecosystem by putting back one missing piece. Ecosystems that have been altered for a long time can settle into a new condition, and pulling one lever may not move them back.
item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Ecology] What is the lecturer's purpose in discussing the wolf story?
choices: To add complications to it without rejecting it
To prove that wolves had no effect on the park
To show that elk were the main cause of river changes
To argue that wolves should be removed from the park
item.correct_answer: To add complications to it without rejecting it
item.explanation: 'I want to complicate that story, not to debunk it.'

distractor_rationales.choice: To prove that wolves had no effect on the park
distractor_rationales.reason: 'There's good evidence that wolves matter.'

distractor_rationales.choice: To show that elk were the main cause of river changes
distractor_rationales.reason: The lecture does not single out elk as the main cause.

distractor_rationales.choice: To argue that wolves should be removed from the park
distractor_rationales.reason: No removal is proposed.
